raw_text:
The transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) has long been the gold standard for the prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) [1]. However, TV-ICDs are associated with significant acute and long-term complications, predominantly related to the transvenous lead [2]. Lead fractures, venous thrombosis, systemic infections, and endocarditis represent major clinical challenges that increase morbidity and mortality [3,4]. To address these hardware-related vulnerabilities, the subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed [5]. By utilizing an entirely extra-cardiovascular design, the S-ICD avoids the risks of vascular access, cardiac perforation, and systemic bloodstream infection, offering a valuable alternative for selected patients [6,7].

The S-ICD system consists of a pulse generator implanted in a left lateral thoracic pocket and a subcutaneous lead positioned parasternally [8,9]. Since the system lacks direct contact with the myocardium, it relies on far-field sensing of cardiac signals. To prevent inappropriate therapies resulting from T-wave oversensing (TWOS), candidates must undergo a mandatory pre-implantation electrocardiographic (ECG) screening using a dedicated template or automated screening tool [10,11]. Successful screening ensures that the QRS-to-T-wave ratio is favorable across multiple vectors [12]. However, the lack of permanent pacing capability remains a primary limitation; the S-ICD cannot deliver anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP), bradycardia pacing (except for post-shock pacing), or cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) [13,14]. 

The clinical efficacy and safety of the S-ICD have been evaluated across various registries and trials [15]. Early registry data, including the prospective EFFORTLESS registry and the US S-ICD Post-Approval Study, demonstrated high rates of successful shock conversion for ventricular fibrillation (VF) and low complication rates [16,17]. The landmark PRAETORIAN trial, a randomized, controlled, non-inferiority trial comparing S-ICD directly to TV-ICD, met its primary endpoint, demonstrating that the S-ICD was non-inferior regarding the combined endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [18]. Although the S-ICD group experienced fewer lead-related complications, it had a slightly higher incidence of inappropriate shocks, primarily due to oversensing [19]. To evaluate strategies for reducing inappropriate shocks, the prospective UNTOUCHED trial utilized modern programming (high-rate cutoffs and the Smart Pass filter) and reported remarkably low rates of inappropriate shocks, comparable to or lower than those seen in contemporary TV-ICD trials [20,21].

Inappropriate shocks, while mitigated by advanced filtering algorithms like the "Smart Pass" and dual-zone programming, remain a clinical concern [22,23]. Pocket infections and hematomas are the most common acute complications, though they rarely lead to systemic infection or require lead extraction via open-heart surgery, unlike TV-ICDs [24,25]. In terms of extraction, removing an S-ICD is vastly simpler and carries significantly lower risk [26]. Recent advances aim to overcome the therapeutic gaps of the S-ICD. The integration of the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker represents a major milestone [27]. This modular system allows the S-ICD to communicate wirelessly with an intra-cardiac leadless pacemaker to deliver ATP or bradycardia pacing when needed, without compromising the extra-cardiovascular benefits of the S-ICD [28,29]. Finally, ongoing refinements continue to evaluate intermuscular pocket placement to optimize cosmetic outcomes and patient comfort [30].

In conclusion, the S-ICD has transitioned from a niche alternative to a standard-of-care therapy for a broad cohort of patients at risk for SCD who do not require pacing. With robust clinical trial backing, refined sensing algorithms, and future modular pacing integrations, the S-ICD represents a paradigm shift in device therapy, balancing effective defibrillation with an improved long-term safety profile.
